questions.question: Tectonite fabric.
questions.solution_html:
• Tectonite fabric - Tectonite fabric is the preferred arrangement of mineral grains, clasts, or
  • structural elements produced by directed stress and deformation in a rock. It may be planar
  • (foliation),linear(lineation),oracombinationofboth.Fabricrecordstheorientationandstyleof
  • deformationandisusefulininterpretingtectonichistory.
  • Strike-slip faults: Net slip is approximately parallel to strike and horizontal. In a right-lateral
  • (dextral) fault, the opposite block appears to move to the right; in a left-lateral (sinistral) fault, it
  • appearstomovetotheleft.
  • Phyllitic foliation: Characteristic of phyllite, with a silky sheen and wavy surfaces. It forms as
  • fine mica and chlorite grains grow or become aligned during low- to moderate-grade
  • metamorphism. The minerals are larger than in slate but generally too fine to be readily
  • distinguishedindividually.

questions.question: Hanging wall and footwall.
questions.solution_html:
• Hanging wall and footwall - In an inclined fault, the hanging wall is the rock mass above the
  • fault plane, while the footwall is the rock mass below it. These terms are geometric and do not
  • by themselves indicate the direction of movement. In a normal fault the hanging wall moves
  • downrelativetothefootwall;inareversefaultitmovesup.
  • Oblique-slip faults: Movement has both dip-slip and strike-slip components. They combine
  • verticalandhorizontaldisplacementandmayreflectmorecomplexstressconditions.Thesense
  • of net slip is determined from displaced markers, slickensides, steps on fault surfaces, drag
  • structures,andotherkinematicindicators.
  • Schistosity: A well-developed foliation caused by the parallel alignment of visible platy or
  • elongate minerals,commonly mica, chlorite, or amphibole. It is typical of schist and commonly
  • develops at medium metamorphic grades through mineral growth, rotation, and deformation.
  • Therocksplitsalongmineral-richplanes.

questions.question: Parallel fold.
questions.solution_html:
• Parallelfold- Aparallelfoldis afoldinwhichthe thickness of abed, measuredperpendicular
  • to bedding, remains approximately constant around the fold. The beds are therefore
  • approximately parallel to one another through the folded structure.Parallel folds are commonly
  • describedasconcentricfoldsandcontrastwithsimilarfolds,inwhichlayerthicknessmeasured
  • perpendiculartotheaxialplaneisapproximatelyconstant.
  • Gneissic banding: A compositional foliation consisting of alternating light-coloured quartz

questions.question: Stratigraphic hiatus.
questions.solution_html:
• Stratigraphic hiatus. - A stratigraphic hiatus is a gap in the geological record representing a
  • periodduringwhichsedimentswerenotdeposited,orpreviouslydepositedmaterialwaseroded.
  • It may be recognized as a break in succession and can be associated with an unconformity.
  • Hiatusesareimportantbecausetheyindicatemissingtimeintherockrecord.
  • Crenulation cleavage: A new cleavage formed when an earlier foliation is folded into small
  • scale crenulations during a later deformation. The new cleavage commonly develops
  • approximately parallel to the axial planes of the microfolds. It is evidence of polyphase
  • deformation.

questions.question: Plunge.
questions.solution_html:
• Plunge - Plunge is the angle that a linear geological feature such as a fold hinge, mineral
  • lineation, or intersection line—makes with the horizontal, measured in a vertical plane. It is
  • describedtogetherwithatrendorbearing.

  • deformation, grain-size reduction, recrystallisation, and mineral alignment. It is commonly
  • associated with shear zones and may occur with stretching lineation and compositional
  • banding.
  • Origin and significance: Foliation can form by mineral alignment, rotation and recrystallisation
  • flattening, pressure solution, metamorphic differentiation, or ductile shearing. Its orientation
  • relative to bedding, fold axial planes,lineation, and shear-sense indicators helps reconstruct
  • deformation events. Not every planar feature has the same origin; primarybedding andtectonic
  • foliationshouldbedistinguishedusingfieldrelationshipsandpetrography.

questions.question: Effect of temperature on deformation.
questions.solution_html:
• Effect of temperature on deformation.- Increasing temperature generally promotes ductile
  • deformation by facilitating crystal plasticity, recrystallization, and diffusion. Rocks may deform
  • at lower differential stress and show less brittle fracturing. At lower temperatures and shallow
  • crustal levels, deformation is more commonly brittle. The response also depends on pressure
  • strainrate,mineralcomposition,fluids,andtime.

questions.question: Systematic joints.
questions.solution_html:
• Systematic joints.- Systematic joints are fractures that occur in organized sets with broadly
  • consistent orientation and spacing.Individual joints in a set are commonly approximately
  • parallel. They may form due to tectonic stress, cooling,unloading, or other processes. Two or
  • more intersecting sets can divide rock into blocks and influence weathering,groundwater flow
  • andengineeringstability.

questions.question: Differentiate the major types of stress and strain in rocks.
questions.solution_html:
• Stress is force per unit area acting within a rock, whereas strain is the change in shape
  • or size produced by deformation.Types of stress: (1) Compression acts to shorten a
  • rockandcommonlyproducesfolds,reversefaults,andthrusts.(2)Tensionor extension
  • stress acts parallel to a surface and causes adjacent parts of a rock to slide past one
  • another. Lithostatic pressure acts approximately equally in all directions and differs
  • from differential stress.Types of strain: (1) Elastic strain is recoverable when stress is
  • removed.(2)Plasticorductilestrainispermanentandmayproducefolds,cleavage,and
  • mineral fabrics. (3) Brittle strain involves fracture and displacement, forming joints and
  • faults. (4) Volumetric strain is a change in volume while distortional strain changes
  • shape. Finite strain may be described as shortening, extension, or shear and may be
  • homogeneousorheterogeneous.
